title: #68 Phil Rosenzweig: The Halo Effect
summary: Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Raddai. I'm your host, Adipalmian and with me in the studio is my friend and colleague, Niklas Savos. In this episode we are delighted to have Phil Rosensvig on the show.

positions.commentary: The speaker discusses Cisco as an example of the halo effect, noting it was the most valued company before the bubble burst and lost 80% of its market share, but states the story is not about Cisco itself.
The speaker mentions Apple as a past example of the most admired company for many years in a row, noting it was in the top five for just about everything.
The speaker expresses suspicion about Nvidia's reputation carrying over to all kinds of other things, doubting they are good at everything despite doing extraordinarily well on AI chips.
The speaker bought Microsoft stock in 1991 and still holds it, expressing satisfaction with the investment.
The speaker describes HP as a great, progressive, and enlightened company during his time there.
The speaker notes that Intel has suffered in recent years but finds Andy Grove's book 'only the paranoid survive' wonderful and suggests the basic lessons are very good.

thesis: This episode argues that the 'halo effect' causes investors to overvalue companies based on past performance or rankings, leading to severe market corrections when attributions change. The speaker illustrates this with examples like Cisco and GE, where the market's perception of greatness was disconnected from the company's actual reality or the speaker's personal doubts.

claims.quote: Cisco for a few weeks at the beginning of 2000 before the internet bubble burst was the most valued company in the world and then lost 80% of its market share and again my story is not about Cisco it's about the way we thought about Cisco and the extraordinary hype that praised Cisco in the late 90s up until 2000 and then the way it was talked about after that
